v: An EPIC that works whether you grew up worshipping Savitri or barely knew her name. Nag Ashwin pulls you into the black-and-white era, Keerthy and Dulquer LIVE their roles, and three hours disappear in a heart full of emotion.
e: Mahanati succeeds with every kind of viewer I could imagine: people who lived through Savitri’s aura, later generations who knew the legend from family and films, and complete newcomers simply looking for a cinematic experience. Nag Ashwin’s narrative, the period craft, Samantha’s climax and astonishing lead performances make it a wonderful, deeply emotional experience.
body:
To start with, I think the audience for Mahanati can roughly be divided into three groups.

The first is the older generation who actually lived through Savitri’s aura and want to see how today’s filmmakers have recreated that legend on screen.

The second is a slightly younger generation who may not have experienced her peak first-hand but still grew up knowing who Savitri was — a little like today’s kids knowing Chiranjeevi even if they did not witness his earliest years.

And then there is the third group: people who may have absolutely no idea who Savitri was and are not emotionally invested in her legacy at all. They simply entered the theatre for a cinematic experience.

The beauty of this EPIC is that all three groups can get glued to the film within the first twenty minutes and leave the auditorium with a heart full of emotions!!!!!

The first two groups will probably see it as a great tribute to a legendary actress.

The third group can enjoy it almost like a film-industry rise-and-fall drama in the emotional space of something like Madhur Bhandarkar’s Fashion, only surrounded by the gorgeous aura of 1950s and 1960s cinema.

Irrespective of your perspective, the film keeps you involved right through the rolling titles, and its long runtime never really feels long.

The director, cinematographer, dialogue writer and BGM composer make sure the audience gets lost in the beauty of that black-and-white era 🙏

Rather than narrating Savitri’s biography in a simple straight line, Nag Ashwin cleverly mixes it with the journey of a journalist, and that structural choice adds another layer to the film.

The opening itself gives you an idea of what kind of experience is coming.

And the climax — with superb dialogues and Samantha’s performance — is an absolute standout 🙏🙏🙏

Keerthy Suresh and Dulquer Salmaan do not merely play Savitri and Gemini Ganesan; they LIVE those characters.

Haa… I could keep writing about this movie, but I still would not be able to put 100% of the emotions I went through while watching it into words.

Thanks, Nag Ashwin, for the wonderful experience.

You dreamt about this biopic and made it big… VERY, VERY BIG!!!

v: A father wanting to send his son to an old-age home — when did we last get a premise this wonderfully strange and meaningful? Instead of a tear-fest, Amitabh and Rishi give us 100 minutes of genuine laughs with emotion quietly running underneath.
e: 102 Not Out proves that strong writing and execution can do wonders without a huge canvas. Amitabh Bachchan and Rishi Kapoor are effortless, but the real stars are Umesh Shukla and writer Saumya Joshi, who turn a potentially heart-wrenching three-character story into a warm, funny and emotionally lasting experience.
body:
Amitabh Bachchan and Rishi Kapoor are at that stage of their careers where they can choose scripts because the subject emotionally moves them or simply interests them — without worrying too much about so-called fan expectations or box-office formulas.

And here they have picked a subject that leaves a genuine emotional impact on the audience.

The script never really has to challenge the acting abilities of these two legends.

At this point, performances like these almost look effortless for them.

But it is the content and execution that keep you glued to the screen.

Come on… when was the last time we came across a story even half as unusual and meaningful as a father wanting to send his own son to an old-age home? 🙏

Given that premise, you might expect a heart-wrenching emotional ride packed with tears.

Instead, what we get is roughly one hour and forty minutes of genuine laughs with a constant undercurrent of emotion and message.

That balance is what I loved.

The story essentially revolves around only three major characters, and these are exactly the kinds of films that make you curious about the people behind the writing and direction rather than merely the star cast.

So full credit to director Umesh Shukla and writer Saumya Joshi.

Kudos to both of you for reminding us that superb content with a modest budget can still do wonders!!!!!

v: A commercialised BLOCKBUSTER version of Leader! I may question how fresh Koratala’s core idea is, but once he layers in Mahesh’s intensity, terrific dialogues, DSP and perfectly placed elevations, the formula works effortlessly.
e: Bharath Ane Nenu did not win me over through originality; I felt Koratala Siva was drawing heavily from the political climate and films such as Leader. But he packages those familiar ideas extremely well, blending commercial hero elevations into the story, giving Mahesh Babu one of his strongest recent vehicles and tapping directly into audience frustration with politics and TRP-driven media.
body:
To start with, I have never been a huge fan of Koratala Siva’s core story ideas.

I often feel he observes what is happening around him, finds a socially relevant idea and then fills it with commercial ingredients.

With Srimanthudu, for example, I personally saw echoes of the village-adoption conversations happening around schemes such as Sansad Adarsh Gram Yojana.

With Janatha Garage, the environmental angle reminded me of initiatives such as Haritha Haram, while parts of the hero-versus-system setup felt familiar from older RGV-style formulas.

Now coming to Bharath Ane Nenu…

My feeling — and this is only my point of view 😄 — is that Koratala looked at the political environment around us, watched something in the space of Leader, and bingo… the broad story foundation was ready.

But once that foundation is in place, he focuses completely on what he does very well: commercial packaging and hero elevation.

The elevation templates may remind you of Srimanthudu and Janatha Garage, yet they blend into this story effortlessly.

And there we go… a BLOCKBUSTER is ready!!!!!

This was obviously the best Mahesh Babu movie I had seen in quite some time.

The audience also connects instantly because so many of us were already vexed with the real political environment and with media houses forever chasing TRPs.

The film has some of the best dialogues I had heard in recent Telugu cinema.

Mahesh is intense as usual, and DSP’s music once again gives the material exactly the kind of commercial energy it needs.

In one sentence: Bharath Ane Nenu is a commercialised, BLOCKBUSTER version of Leader!!!!!

v: It may disappoint viewers expecting Sukumar’s usual intellectual games or anyone allergic to a three-hour runtime — but watch it for Charan, Samantha, Aadhi, Jagapathi Babu, Naresh and that gorgeous 1980s Godavari world, and there is plenty to LOVE.
e: Rangasthalam is less about Sukumar showing off clever narrative tricks and more about performances and world-building. The long runtime may test some viewers, but the cast is excellent, the 1980s Godavari village is beautifully realised, DSP’s BGM and meaningful songs add enormous flavour, and Ram Charan finally gets to show the actor inside the star.
body:
Rangasthalam may disappoint you if you are a huge fan of Sukumar’s more overtly intelligent, puzzle-like direction.

And it may definitely disappoint you if you are too impatient to sit through a movie whose runtime is close to three hours.

On the other hand, you can love this movie to the core if you watch it for the performances.

Ram Charan, Samantha, Aadhi, Jagapathi Babu and Naresh are all EXCELLENT.

You can also love the film simply for the excellent recreation of a 1980s Godavari village.

The world feels lived-in, textured and completely different from the polished commercial settings we usually get.

DSP’s BGM is terrific as usual, while the songs come with meaningful lyrics that genuinely add value to the atmosphere and characters.

Special shout-out to “Aa Gattununtava”, which has excellent lyrics but somehow did not become as dominant as the other chartbusters.

And finally, after almost a decade in films, Ram Charan really shows the audience what he can do as an actor.

This is the kind of performance that should make the ACTOR Chiranjeevi — not merely the Megastar or one of Telugu cinema’s greatest dancers — feel proud 🙏

I only hope Charan continues choosing scripts that give him this kind of opportunity.
